content: Geology is the scientific study of the Earth, encompassing its composition, structure, physical properties, history, and the dynamic processes that shape it. The term geology originates from the Greek words gemeaning the Earth and logos meaning word or reason. Geologists have determined that the Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old. They have also discovered that tectonic plates move atop a viscous layer of the mantle, forming the Earth's crust. Geologists play a critical role in locating and managing natural resources, such as oil. The principles of geology are also applied to other celestial bodies in the solar system, a field known as astrogeology. Specific terms like selenology (the study of the Moon) and areology (the study of Mars) are used for specialized branches of astrogeology. The history of geology includes significant contributions from early pioneers. Georg Agricola (1494–1555) authored the first systematic work on mining and smelting, titled De re metallica libri XII, published in 1556. This work addressed topics such as wind and hydrodynamic energy, ore transportation, and the extraction of materials like sulfur and alum. James Hutton, often regarded as the father of modern geology, presented his groundbreaking paper Theory of the Earth in 1785 to the Royal Society of Edinburgh. Hutton proposed that the Earth was far older than previously believed, allowing sufficient time for processes like mountain erosion and sediment deposition to occur. His followers, known as plutonists, argued that some rocks formed through volcanic activity, in contrast to the neptunists, who believed all rocks originated from a receding ocean. William Smith (1769–1839) created some of the earliest geological maps and pioneered the classification of rock layers (strata) based on their fossil content. Sir Charles Lyell, in his seminal work Principles of Geology (first published in 1830), championed the concept of uniformitarianism. This theory posits that slow, consistent geological processes have shaped the Earth over time and continue to do so today. Uniformitarianism stood in opposition to catastrophism, which suggested that Earth's features were formed by sudden, singular events. Although Hutton supported uniformitarianism, it was not widely accepted during his time. The theory of continental drift was introduced by Alfred Wegener in 1912 and later supported by Arthur Holmes. However, it did not gain widespread acceptance until the 1960s, when the theory of plate tectonics provided a robust framework for understanding the movement of Earth's lithospheric plates. Geology encompasses numerous sub-disciplines, each focusing on specific aspects of the Earth and its processes. These include economic geology, environmental geology, geochemistry, geochronology, geodetics, geomicrobiology, geomorphology, geophysics, glaciology, hydrogeology (or geohydrology), marine geology, mineralogy, paleoclimatology, paleontology, pedology (the study of soils), petroleum geology, petrology, sedimentology, seismology, stratigraphy, structural geology, tectonics, and volcanology. Engineering geology, which supports civil and geotechnical engineering, is distinct from geological engineering. Geological engineers are licensed as engineers, while engineering geologists are licensed as geologists. Regional geology focuses on specific areas, such as the geology of the Alps or the glacial geology of the Genesee River in New York and Pennsylvania. National geology examines the geological characteristics of entire countries or regions, such as the geology of Australia, Victoria, the United States, California, the Grand Canyon area, and the United Kingdom.
